items.text: All that we are is the result of what we have thought; it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts.
Hatred does not cease by hatred at any time; hatred ceases by love. This is an old rule.
Not the faults of others, but one's own misdeeds and negligences, should a wise person take notice of.
There is no suffering for one who has finished the journey, let go of grief, and thrown off every fetter.
Though one conquers a thousand thousand enemies in battle, the one who conquers oneself is the greater victor.
Self is the lord of self; who else could be the lord?
"He abused me, he beat me, he defeated me, he robbed me" — in those who do not harbour such thoughts, hatred will cease.
Better than a thousand senseless words is one word of sense, which, when heard, brings quiet.
Let go of anger, let go of pride, and rise above all bondage. No suffering touches one who clings to nothing and calls nothing their own.
Let a man overcome anger by love; let him overcome evil by good; let him overcome the greedy by liberality, the liar by truth.
The fault of others is easy to see; one's own fault is hard to see.
Do not think lightly of good, saying in your heart, It will not come near me. Even by falling water-drops a water-pot is filled; the wise become full of good, even if they gather it little by little.
From one who overcomes this fierce thirst, sufferings fall away, like water-drops from a lotus leaf.
As a tree, even when cut down, grows again if its root remains unharmed, so pain returns again and again unless the root of craving is destroyed.
Wise people call that the strong fetter which drags one down and is hard to undo; having cut it, one leaves behind desire and pleasure, free from care.
The highest excellence is like that of water. It benefits all things, and does not strive; it is content with the low place that others dislike.
items.source: Tao Te Ching, ch. 8 (after Legge's 1891 translation)

items.text: It is better to leave a vessel unfilled than to carry it full. When the work is done and one's name made, to withdraw is the way of Heaven.
items.source: Tao Te Ching, ch. 9 (after Legge's 1891 translation)

items.text: Favour and disgrace are equally to be feared; for the getting of favour brings the fear of losing it.
items.source: Tao Te Ching, ch. 13 (after Legge's 1891 translation)

items.text: He who overcomes others is strong; he who overcomes himself is mighty. He who is satisfied with his lot is rich.
items.source: Tao Te Ching, ch. 33 (after Legge's 1891 translation)

items.text: Who is content needs fear no shame; who knows when to stop incurs no blame, and remains free from danger.
items.source: Tao Te Ching, ch. 44 (after Legge's 1891 translation)

items.text: There is no greater calamity than discontent with one's lot, and no greater fault than the wish for more; the sufficiency of contentment is an enduring sufficiency.
items.source: Tao Te Ching, ch. 46 (after Legge's 1891 translation)

items.text: Blunt the sharp points, unravel the complications; temper the brightness, and come into agreement with the obscurity of others.
items.source: Tao Te Ching, ch. 56 (after Legge's 1891 translation)

items.text: At birth, a person is supple and weak; in old age, firm and stiff. Softness is a mark of being alive; stiffness, a mark of decline.
items.source: Tao Te Ching, ch. 76 (after Legge's 1891 translation)

items.text: No one can fix on me what is ugly, nor can I be angry with my kinsman, nor hate him; for we are made for co-operation.
Of human life the time is a point, and the substance is in a flux; everything which belongs to the body is a stream, and what belongs to the soul is a dream and a vapor.
Nowhere does a man retire with more quiet or more freedom from trouble than into his own soul; and tranquillity is nothing else than the good ordering of the mind.
Time is like a river made up of the events which happen; as soon as a thing has been seen, it is carried away, and another comes in its place.
If thou art pained by any external thing, it is not this thing that disturbs thee, but thy own judgment about it. And it is in thy power to wipe out this judgment now.
It is not men's acts that disturb us, but our own opinions about them. Take away these opinions, dismiss the judgment, and your anger is gone.
How ridiculous, and what a stranger, is one who is surprised at anything that happens in life.
